entry.evidence: Most of the time, RS cannot simulate spatio-temporal variability of rainfall like natural rainfall events

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

steps.action: Framed the gap from the literature: most hydrological experiments assume a stationary, instantaneous storm and so ignore storm movement, which may bias runoff peak estimates.
steps.quote: Thus, such hydrological studies ignore the effect of storm movement on catchment runoff response.

steps.action: Stated two qualitative expected behaviours as evaluation criteria for the simulator: a downstream-moving storm should give higher Qp and lower tp than an upstream-moving storm. Later text attributes the same result to de Lima and Singh (2003) and others.
steps.quote: Time to peak ( t p ) of the downstream directional storm should be lower than the upstream directional storm

steps.action: Built the programmable moving-storm rainfall simulator. Components: a 3 m x 2 m frame with 11 full-cone nozzles in four clusters; servo-operated valves driven by an Arduino Mega through a Bluetooth module and an Android app; a PID-controlled bypass globe valve to hold constant line pressure; and a tiltable 2.5 m x 1.44 m soil flume with surface, subsurface and deep outlets (detail in §2.1 to §2.5, Tables 1, Figures 1 to 7).
steps.quote: These clusters were activated and deactivated with a specific time gap to simulate the moving storm over the plot area.

steps.action: Designed the test: 12 scenarios (2 slopes x 3 velocities x 2 directions), three replications each, on a fully saturated bed. Planned a multiple regression of tp and Qp on direction (indicator), velocity and slope, testing null coefficients at the 5 % level (§2.7 ¶2).
steps.quote: Experiments were performed under fully saturated soil bed conditions to reduce the variability among scenarios and replications.

steps.action: Checked rainfall uniformity with 66 beakers on a 250 mm grid (Christiansen UC, §2.6 ¶1), giving UC 84.2 % and edge deficits. Compared this with published simulators (UC 75 % to 94 %), and compared the 40 mm/h intensity with natural 5 min maxima in the Aglar watershed.
steps.quote: However, the overall UC was found to be 84.2 %.

steps.action: Ran the moving-storm scenarios at 2.5 % slope. The 6 m/min velocity produced non-detectable runoff and was dropped from the results.
steps.quote: For the velocity of 6 m min - 1 , non-detectable runoff was generated and, therefore, it was not included in the result.

steps.action: Recorded overland-flow hydrographs at the flume outlet for 2 and 3 m/min storms moving in both directions at 2.5 % slope.
steps.quote: Hydrograph for velocity 2 m min - 1 (a) and 3 m min - 1 (b) at 2.5 % slope.

steps.action: Compared the hydrographs with the expected behaviour: tp was shorter for the downstream-moving storm at both velocities. Explained this by runoff travelling with the storm toward the outlet.
steps.quote: storm was less than the downstream to the upstream storm irrespective of their velocities

steps.action: Observed a 110 s longer recession for the upstream-moving storm at 2 m/min, a negligible difference at 3 m/min, and 150 s longer recession at 2 m/min than at 3 m/min for upstream storms. Noted the similarity with de Lima and Singh (2003).
steps.quote: displays a 110 s longer recession time compared to the opposite storm movement especially during low storm velocity

steps.action: Repeated the scenarios at 5 % slope with 2, 3 and 6 m/min storms and found the same recession, tp and Qp trends as at 2.5 %.
steps.quote: followed the same trend as the hydrographs generated at 2.5 % slope

steps.action: Observed that at 6 m/min and 5 % slope the recession curve and Qp of the upstream and downstream storms coincided, with only tp differing slightly.
steps.quote: the recession curve and Q p of both hydrographs completely matched with each other

steps.action: Compared scenario values (Table 3). Qp was 42.8 % to 59 % higher at 5 % than at 2.5 % slope and fell with storm velocity; discharge volume followed the same pattern (§3.2 ¶3).
steps.quote: These analyses concluded that the Q p value increases significantly with an increase in soil flume slope and decreases with increased storm velocity.

steps.action: Set the results against published moving-storm experiments: smaller runoff at high velocity, no direction effect at high velocity, runoff rising with slope, and higher Qp for downstream storms (de Lima and Singh 2003; de Lima et al. 2011; Isidoro et al. 2012; Seo and Schmidt 2013). Reported agreement.
steps.quote: They concluded that the downstream storm produces higher Q p than the upstream directional storm.

steps.action: Fitted two multiple regression models (tp and Qp) on storm direction (indicator, upstream = 1), velocity and slope, giving coefficients with standard errors (Table 4).

Tested the coefficients against the null of zero effect at the 5 % level. Direction raised tp by 10 s and lowered Qp by 0.00256 L/s, both significant; R2 was 0.89 and 0.94; the coefficient signs agreed with the empirical trends.
steps.quote: These values are significant at 5 % level of significance, thus, providing a satisfactory hydrological verification for the moving storm rainfall simulator.

steps.action: Kept the claim that the simulator generates moving-storm conditions satisfactorily. Stated the limits: a single storm pattern, two slopes, two directions and three velocities.
steps.quote: it is evident that the tool could generate the moving storm condition satisfactorily

steps.action: Kept four hydrological conclusions: downstream storms give a higher, sharper peak and shorter recession; upstream storms give a lower peak and prolonged recession; the direction effect becomes negligible at high velocity; and steeper slope reduces the direction effect.
steps.quote: The hydrograph generated from the downstream moving storms yielded a higher peak with a sharp rise and short recession limb

tree.answer: Storm movement direction and velocity alter runoff hydrographs; already reported in the literature
Hydrographs are measured directly at the flume outlet, but only once a moving-storm simulator exists
Build a programmable simulator that reproduces moving storms and show that it works
No substantive rivals; only the regression null of no effect of direction, velocity or slope
Expected direction effects (higher Qp, lower tp downstream) against the null of no effect
Conditions set in the laboratory: slope, storm velocity and direction on a saturated bed
Same trends at a second slope; three replications per scenario; agreement with published experiments
Simulator judged to generate moving storms satisfactorily; direction coefficients significant at 5 %
No review file supplied; review history not documented

end.claim: The programmable multi-nozzle simulator generates moving-storm rainfall (UC 84.2 %, 40 mm/h) that reproduces the expected hydrograph response: higher Qp and shorter tp for downstream-moving storms, significant at 5 %.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the automated, sequentially switched nozzle clusters and constant-pressure control there would be no moving-storm experiments to evaluate.

gates.evidence: Action: the two expected behaviours (§1 ¶5) shaped the upstream/downstream scenario design, but the data were collected to show the instrument works, not to test a hydrological hypothesis. Claim: the simulator could have failed to reproduce the expected direction effect, and the regression null could have stood (§3.2 ¶7). However, the criteria are qualitative with no tolerances, and a no-runoff case (6 m/min, 2.5 %) was dropped (§3.1 ¶1). Registration: criteria and the 5 % level are stated in the paper, but nothing shows they were fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Arduino Mega microcontroller with SoftwareSerial and Servo libraries
HC-05 Bluetooth module for wireless valve control
PID controller (Selec PID500) with pressure transmitter and motorised bypass globe valve
Android app built with MIT App Inventor ('MIT app developer')
Multiple regression with an indicator variable and t-tests of coefficients

limits:
1. Sources. No review file or discussion was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded. The paper makes no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' claim, so novelty_claims is empty.

2. Unreported checks of the apparatus.
- The pressure-regulating system is meant to keep intensity constant while clusters switch (§2.2.1 ¶3), but no pressure or intensity record during switching is reported. Inference: this premise is untested in the text.
- Uniformity was measured only for a static spray (§2.6, §3 ¶1), not for the moving storm.
- There is no stationary-storm control, although the introduction argues that the stationary assumption biases results (§1 ¶4-5).

3. Replication and statistics.
- Three replications are stated (§2.7 ¶1), but Table 3 gives single values per scenario and no between-replicate spread is reported.
- It is unclear whether the regression used 10 scenario values or 30 runs.
- The '±4.776 s' in §3.2 ¶7 against a standard error of 2.32 in Table 4 suggests a 95 % interval half-width. This is inference.

4. Conclusions not tested by the analysis.
- Conclusions 3 and 4 (§4 ¶2) concern how the direction effect changes with velocity and slope. The additive regression has no interaction terms, so it does not test them.
- Conclusion 3 rests on one 6 m/min case at 5 % slope.
- For conclusion 4, Table 3 shows the absolute Qp difference between directions growing with slope (2.1 and 1.7 at 2.5 % vs 5.0 and 4.0 at 5 %), while tp differences shrink. Inference: Qp partly contradicts the conclusion.

5. Inconsistencies in the text.
- Flume dimensions differ between the abstract and §2.2 ¶1.
- The abstract says 'varying spatial and temporal resolutions', but a single intensity was used.

6. Sub-claims and their statuses.
- The hydrological regularities (direction, slope and velocity effects on tp, Qp and recession) are regularity_in_range: 2.5-5 % slope, 2-6 m/min, saturated sandy loam, 40 mm/h, a single storm pattern.
- The regression coefficients are estimate_with_resolution.

7. Coding choices.
- Composition capability_first fits only loosely: the expected behaviours were taken from prior work before the data and serve as calibration targets for the instrument, not as rivals. Because of this, step 2 is coded 'cited'; the published text attributes the same result to others only later (§3.2 ¶5).
- The robustness check (5 % slope) varies an experimental factor rather than an auxiliary.

disagreements.target: Most hydrological experimental methods that assume the rainstorm reaches the catchment instantaneously and stays steady (Singh, 1998)
disagreements.support: The authors argue from Wilson et al. (1979) that ignoring storm movement can misestimate runoff peaks, and show direction effects in their flume. They include no stationary-storm comparison.
disagreements.quote: An important assumption underlying most hydrological experimental methods is that the rainstorm reaches instantaneously over the catchment and remains [...]

disagreements.target: Rainfall simulation studies that treat rainfall intensity as constant in space and time
disagreements.support: The authors assert that such inferences may be unrepresentative and offer the moving-storm simulator as the remedy. They show no direct comparison with constant-intensity runs.
disagreements.quote: Inferences from such studies may not be representative of the actual process underway.
